title: Analysis of Helsinki city bike traffic data
text:
Every day thousands of people in Helsinki make their commute by bicycle, and many of them use city bikes found across the city. It has become a core way to get around in Helsinki. However, the users of city bikes sometimes face different problems when using the bikes: empty station when wanting to use a bike, full station when returning a bike or problems with using bikes.
This data science project analyzes nine seasons of city bike trip records in Helsinki from 2017 to 2025. We use the publicly available dataset published by HSL. The project examines station departures and returns, trip volumes over time, and the patterns that emerge from the data. We also present our insights and recommendations for HSL based on our analysis.
Cycling eases congestion and air pollution while giving residents of Helsinki an affordable and healthy way to navigate in the city. To realize these benefits, cycling needs to be a convenient choice for residents. Our aim is to analyze the data so that it can be used to make decisions on investing in the current bike infrastructure in Helsinki and improving logistics.

title: Analysis of Helsinki city bike traffic data
text:
Trip data



Figure 1: Durations of all city bike trips for years 2017-2025.


Over nine seasons, a total of 22 million trips were made. When a season starts, the volume of trips starts to increase and peaks most years around June and July after which the volume decreases towards the end of the season. Significant portion of trips were under 20 minutes as seen in figure 1. Ride distance and velocity had a wider distribution, with the average distance and velocity being around 1km and 11 km/h respectively.



Figure 2: Hourly trip volume for years 2017-2025.


Hourly trip volume reveals a distinct bimodal commuter rhythm seen in figure 2. Demand surges during the morning peak between 07:00 and 09:00 as commuters head to offices and universities. Traffic remains steady through the midday, and reaches its highest volume during the evening peak between 15:00 and 18:00 (peaking around 16:30) as workers return home.



Figure 3: Rides with distance between 25 and 200 meters.


During data cleaning, we identified short round-trips where a user returned the bike to the same station within 3 minutes and covered under 100 meters. These indicate faulty bikes, slipping gears, or dock release errors. Our analysis revealed that 2.7% to 7.2% of all annual trips (59,000 to 203,000 trips each year) are hardware disturbances, providing a valuable metric for dock and fleet maintenance. Figure 3 shows the volume of trips where traveled distance was small.

Multi-Year Evolution (2017–2025)

2017–2019: Early adoption grew rapidly from 1.59 million rides in 2017 to a record of 3.18 million rides in 2019.
2020: During the COVID-19 pandemic, ridership dropped to 2.63 million due to remote work and distance learning.
2021: The system expanded significantly into northern and eastern neighborhoods, recording 2.44 million trips.
2022–2025: The network matured into a steady equilibrium, reliably handling between 2.11 million and 2.23 million trips each year.

title: Analysis of Helsinki city bike traffic data
text:
Stations



Figure 4: Average change in capacity at the most popular bike stations.


We inspected how bike station capacity changes between stations. Fig 4. has a heatmap of average hourly capacity change in the 10 busiest stations. We see that even though some stations have a high volume of traffic, the capacity remains reasonably stable. Some stations lose bikes in the morning and receive bikes in the evening; some stations experience the opposite. Most significant capacity change also does not always happen during the busiest hours. Some stations lose or gain overall a significant number of bikes during the day. Pasilan Asema bike station had the largest ratio of departures over arrivals. This implies a lot of people arrive at Pasila train station via other means but leave with a city bike. Holidays also affect capacity. The largest instance of more bikes arriving over leaving happens at Esplanadi during the first of May where the Labor Day celebrations are held.



Figure 5: Departures and returns at 15 most used stations.


By reverse-geocoding all 347 stations with OpenStreetMap Nominatim, we mapped every station to its 5-digit postal code (00100 Kluuvi, 00180 Kamppi, 00530 Kallio, etc.). Aggregating departures from 2017 to 2025 shows the top 5 busiest hubs across Helsinki: - Itämerentori (Ruoholahti) — Top station in the network with over 453,000 departures. - Töölönlahdenkatu & Central Railway Station (Rautatientori) — Primary rail/metro transfer point with over 385,000 departures. - Ympyrätalo (Hakaniemi) — Dense northern transit gateway. - Kalasatama (M) & Kamppi — Core metro and shopping interchanges.

Insights from data
Using our data on how bike station capacity changes, we were able to create a calculator that estimates bike availability. HSL itself does not currently provide any estimator for bike traffic in their travel planner. Using our data, it would be very easy for them to add estimators beside station capacity amounts.

This tool is useful for end users and HSL alike. If a station has currently few bikes, it is easy to check if it is likely to empty soon. Users can avoid missing out on bikes, and bike relocation can be more preemptive. We do not have data on bike refills or recent trends, so the estimations can often be quite different from reality.



Figure 6: Bike stations clustered by similar traffic.


To understand why stations with similar patterns are close together, we built an Unsupervised Spatial-Constrained Clustering model combining each station’s 6 nearest geographic neighbors with their 24-hour demand curves. This revealed 3 key neighborhood archetypes across Helsinki as seen in figure 6: - Commercial & Transit Sinks (Clusters 0 & 4): Located in Kamppi, Kluuvi, and Ruoholahti. High morning inflows, busy midday turnover, and massive evening outflows. - Residential Commuter Sources (Clusters 3 & 5): Located in Kallio, Alppiharju, and Töölö. High morning departure spikes as residents head to work, followed by evening return accumulation. - Peripheral & Recreational Outposts (Clusters 1 & 2): Flatter diurnal curves with higher weekend and leisure riding.

title: Analysis of Helsinki city bike traffic data
section: What our findings tell to HSL and users
text:
What our findings tell to HSL and users
For Commuters: - While the network is generally reliable, commuters traveling through high-demand hubs (Central Station, Pasila, Itämerentori) during peak rush hours face occasional dock shortages and should keep a backup station in mind. Operational Recommendations for HSL: - Cluster-Based Proactive Rebalancing: Shuttle bikes from Commercial Sinks (Clusters 0 & 4) back to Residential Origins (Clusters 3 & 5) between 13:00 and 15:00, before the evening rush begins. - Automated Disturbance Triage: When a station records 3 or more consecutive trips returned to the same station in under 3 minutes, automatically alert maintenance teams to inspect the dock for damaged latches or faulty bikes. - High-Volume Capacity Upgrades: High-saturation hubs (Itämerentori, Töölönlahdenkatu, and Pasila) should receive expanded dock allocations or overflow drop-zones to prevent full-station return failures.

title: Analysis of Helsinki city bike traffic data
text:
Conclusion
Across 9 seasons and 21.3 million rides, one thing is clear: Helsinki’s city bikes are the heartbeat of the capital’s daily commute. With 85.8% of trips taking under 20 minutes, they aren’t for sightseeing. Instead, they’re fast connectors between homes, metros, and offices. Busiest hubs like Itämerentori and Töölönlahdenkatu face massive rush-hour imbalances every day. By filtering out broken trips and using spatial machine learning, we grouped 347 stations into functional neighborhoods, separating morning residential sources from busy downtown sinks. We then turned these insights into an interactive availability calculator to help riders beat dock congestion and commute with confidence.

title: Analysis of Helsinki city bike traffic data
text:
Project Limitations
While our models offer deep historical insight, the project has a few practical limitations.
- No real-time weather data - Sudden rainfall, wind, and seasonal temperature swings strongly influence cycling volumes, but this weather information is not currently included in our dataset or reflected in our predictions.
- Static station modeling – The models treat stations statically and do not track individual bike maintenance lifecycles. - Delayed Data Updates - The datasets are only updated after the end of the season, meaning we cannot use data during the season to evaluate traffic.
- Unknown station capacity - The measured datapoints are somewhat lacking; we also do not know the capacity of a station at any given time. The public dataset does not record HSL’s manual truck rebalancing logs.

title: Analysis of Helsinki city bike traffic data
text:
Possible Future Analysis
Looking ahead, there are several exciting avenues for future development: - Adding weather Data: add weather information from the Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI) into our prediction model. In Finland, rain and bad weather are the main reasons people decide not to ride bikes so this would make our predictions much more accurate.
- Tracking Metro and Train Delays: Connect live delay and cancellation data from trains and the metro. When trains break down or get delayed at busy stations like Pasila or the Central Railway Station, people rush to grab city bikes instead. Knowing about delays in real time would help predict these sudden spikes in demand.
- Testing AI models: Try more advanced tools (like graph neural networks (GNNs)) that can look the whole city at once and understand how bikes flow from one neighborhood to another throughout the day.
- Planning Better Driving Routes for HSL: develop a tool that plans the best driving routes for city workers who move bikes. It could tell them the fastest way to pick up extra bikes from office areas in the evening and bring them back to residential neighborhoods before the next morning rush.
